Foundations / A global history in development

Humanity’s search for mind.

How have humans tried to answer the question—what is mind?

Through souls and selves, hearts and brains, dreams and experiments. Explore accounts across cultures, religions and disciplines, from evidence before writing to contemporary research.

The overviewExplore 44 accountsCoverage & gapsWords, voices & bodies

The history in brief

Many answers. Different ways of knowing.

“Mind” is our English starting point. The accounts below sometimes concern life, soul, self, attention or personhood instead. Their differences are part of the history.

  1. Explain experience.Dreaming, remembering, suffering and skilled action can lead to very different accounts of a person.
  2. Choose a way to know.Argument, revelation, introspection, cultivation, art and experiment make different kinds of evidence available.
  3. Live with the answer.Accounts of mind can shape education, healing, responsibility and relations with other beings.

An editorial synthesis of the linked accounts. Traditions overlap, disagree internally and continue into the present; this is not a single progression from religion to science.

Recurring approaches

Follow an idea across time. These are editorial comparisons, not fixed categories of peoples.

Explore the history

Grouped by broad period. Dates refer to particular works, objects or documented accounts—not the beginning or end of a culture. BCE and CE use the common calendar era.

01

Before written records

Before writing

Multiple regions · Archaeological evidence

Minds before surviving explanations

Tools, images, instruments and burials preserve evidence of human capacities long before written theories of mind.

Archaeology / Art / Music

Read the account & sources

Making and using objects can reveal planning, skill, social learning and symbolic activity. Archaeologists reason from material traces; those traces rarely specify their makers’ exact account of a self or soul.

Encounter: the Smithsonian’s collection of behavioral evidence, including tools, art and music.

Context & limits. A burial is not a transcript of belief. Living oral traditions are not fossils of prehistory.

02

c. 1550–1200 BCE objects

Ancient accounts

Africa · Egyptian religious traditions

The heart remembers a life

Egyptian heart amulets connect intelligence, feeling, memory and conduct with the heart.

Religion / Art / Medicine

Read the account & sources

In funerary judgment the heart could testify about a person’s deeds. Protecting it was therefore also a concern with identity and moral accountability. An object makes a complex account of the person tangible.

Encounter: New Kingdom heart amulets and the Weighing of the Heart.

Context & limits. The museum account concerns a funerary setting; Egyptian ideas changed across periods and texts.

First millennium BCE textual tradition

Ancient accounts

West Asia & North Africa · Mesopotamian healing traditions

Distress receives names

Akkadian diagnostic texts describe changes in thought and feeling within a medical and religious account of illness.

Medicine / Religion

Read the account & sources

A study of the Diagnostic Handbook traces recurring descriptions translated as depression, heartbreak and an altered mind. Therapeutic texts also invoke ghosts and witchcraft. Symptoms and explanations must be distinguished.

Encounter: descriptions in the Akkadian Diagnostic Handbook, through a specialist study.

Context & limits. Modern translations such as “depression” do not establish equivalence with a modern diagnosis.

04

First millennium BCE; dating debated

Ancient accounts

South Asia · Upanishadic & Hindu traditions

The knowing behind thought

The Kena Upanishad distinguishes the mind’s thinking from that which makes thinking possible.

Philosophy / Religion

Read the account & sources

Knowing is not treated simply as possession of an object. The text directs attention toward Brahman and the limits of ordinary perception and thought. Later Hindu schools interpret self and ultimate reality in substantially different ways.

Great work: Kena Upanishad; compare the Katha Upanishad in the same volume.

Context & limits. The linked 1919 edition is Swami Paramananda’s translation and commentary, with its own theological perspective; its historical introduction is not our dating authority.

05

First millennium BCE onward

Ancient accounts

South Asia · Buddhist traditions

Mental life without a permanent owner

Buddhist accounts analyze changing experience and challenge attachment to an enduring, independent self.

Philosophy / Religion / Psychology

Read the account & sources

Indian Buddhist schools developed different accounts of consciousness, cognition and mental factors. Analysis serves a practical concern: understanding the conditions of suffering and liberation. “No self” does not mean that experiences or ethical consequences simply disappear.

Great works: Dhammapada; Vasubandhu’s Treasury of Higher Knowledge for a later systematic account.

Context & limits. This overview concerns selected Indian Buddhist debates. It cannot stand for all Buddhist schools or later Asian developments.

First millennium BCE onward

Ancient accounts

South Asia · Jain traditions

Living beings as knowing selves

Jain accounts treat living beings as jīvas, selves whose knowledge is obstructed by karmic matter.

Philosophy / Religion / Ethics

Read the account & sources

Liberation involves disentangling the self from karmic bondage. Nonviolence, restraint and knowledge belong to the same project. This differs sharply from Buddhist criticism of a permanent self, despite shared settings and concerns.

Encounter: the Uttarādhyayana and later Jain accounts of knowledge and many-sidedness.

Context & limits. Jain schools and texts differ; “soul” is an approximate translation of jīva.

A bodily explanation of altered experience

On the Sacred Disease argues that the illness it discusses has a natural cause and assigns major mental functions to the brain.

Medicine / Neuroscience

Read the account & sources

Pleasure, sorrow, perception and understanding enter a bodily account. Its physiology is ancient, yet the text demonstrates that natural explanation is not a purely modern invention.

Great work: On the Sacred Disease, in the Hippocratic corpus.

Context & limits. Traditional attribution to Hippocrates does not establish individual authorship. Its account of epilepsy is not current medicine.

Ancient accounts

Europe & Mediterranean · Greek philosophical traditions

The soul contains competing impulses

Plato’s Phaedrus uses a charioteer and two horses to portray tensions within the soul.

Philosophy / Literature

Read the account & sources

Reason, aspiration and unruly desire become intelligible through a dramatic image. The dialogue connects the account with love, beauty and the direction of a life. Its literary form is part of the argument.

Great work: Phaedrus, especially 246a onward.

Context & limits. A philosophical image is not a diagram of anatomical parts. Plato’s dialogues develop more than one account of soul.

Mind belongs within an account of life

Aristotle studies soul through the capacities of living things, including nutrition, perception and thought.

Philosophy / Biology

Read the account & sources

Psychē is broader than modern English “mind.” In On the Soul, the soul is the actuality of a living body, rather than simply another object inside it. The status of intellect introduces further interpretive difficulties.

Context & limits. Calling this either modern materialism or straightforward body–soul dualism loses important distinctions.

Still mental activity to distinguish the seer

Classical Yoga distinguishes changing mental activity from puruṣa, the conscious seer.

Philosophy / Religion / Psychology

Read the account & sources

Citta, often translated as mind, belongs to the changing processes of nature. Concentration and disciplined practice aim at liberation. This distinction makes it especially misleading to translate every relevant term simply as “mind.”

Great work: Patañjali’s Yoga Sūtras, with commentary.

Context & limits. Classical Yoga is a specific philosophical tradition; it is not interchangeable with all Hindu thought or modern postural yoga.

1637 CE

1500–1800

Europe & Mediterranean · Early modern rationalism

The thinker survives radical doubt

Descartes treats the activity of doubting as evidence that the thinking subject exists.

Philosophy

Read the account & sources

In Part IV of the Discourse on Method, he argues for the distinction of thinking mind from body. Doubt is a method for establishing certainty, not simply an expression of indecision. The argument’s later influence does not make it humanity’s first examination of mind.

Great work: Discourse on Method, Part IV; companion Meditations.

Context & limits. Certainty of thinking and the claim that mind is an independent substance are distinct argumentative steps.

The work broadens the experimental study of biological organization. Adaptive coordination can be investigated without assuming that every coordinated system has subjective experience.

Encounter: Revealing non-trivial information structures in aneural biological tissues via functional connectivity.

Context & limits. Functional connectivity is a statistical relationship. Neither network structure nor coordinated repair establishes subjective experience. The sample is small.

  • Blackiston, Dromiack, Grasso and colleagues, including Michael LevinExisting learning-bank record · Abstract and publication record checked.

2019

1950–present

Multiple regions · Contemporary research

Feeling placed at the center

Mark Solms argues for an account of consciousness centered on affect and the regulation of bodily needs.

Neuroscience / Psychology

Read the account & sources

The proposal connects felt experience with the problems a living organism must solve. It is a theoretical position in an active debate, not a consensus definition of consciousness.

Encounter: The Hard Problem of Consciousness and the Free Energy Principle.

Context & limits. A theoretical synthesis. The proposed explanation of subjective experience remains contested; feeling, cognition and cortical processing are not interchangeable terms.

Artificial systems report experience

Cameron Berg and collaborators examine reports of subjective experience produced by language models.

Computing / Psychology / Philosophy

Read the account & sources

Model self-reports can become objects of systematic investigation. Interpreting them requires separating linguistic behavior, experimental conditions and a claim that experience is actually present.

Encounter: Large Language Models Report Subjective Experience Under Self-Referential Processing.

Context & limits. The authors explicitly state that these results are not direct evidence of consciousness. Model self-reports cannot simply be treated as human testimony.

Competing theories face shared tests

An adversarial collaboration tests predictions from global neuronal workspace and integrated information theories.

Read the account & sources

Researchers agree on tests across multiple laboratories and measurement methods. Findings challenge important predictions of both theories. The study makes disagreement experimentally productive rather than announcing a final solution to consciousness.

Context & limits. The experiment tests specified predictions under particular conditions, not every claim of either theory.

Editorial check: 10 October 2026 · Link to this account

Ideas travel through people and materials.

Translation changes the vocabulary

The Arabic philosophical tradition engaged Greek works; its thinkers also developed their own accounts. Translation is an intellectual event, not a transparent transfer of equivalent words.

Mind and print meet in Korea

Jikji’s surviving 1377 metal-type volume makes the material history of Buddhist teachings visible. The history of printed inquiry begins well before a European-only account would suggest.

Contemporary research joins older disputes

Feeling, living organization and artificial systems bring new methods to enduring disagreements. Similar vocabulary does not establish that an ancient text predicted a modern finding.

Global scope. Visible limits.

This edition contains 44 selected accounts. It spans evidence before writing, ancient texts, later religious and philosophical debates, living traditions, arts and modern research. It does not yet represent every culture, religion or discipline. A missing entry marks a gap in this collection, not an absence of thought.

What the sources can establish

Primary texts show particular arguments. Museum records connect objects to documented contexts. Scholarly overviews reconstruct debates. Experiments test specific claims. Each entry identifies its source and review depth; an abstract-level check is not a full-paper review.

Older English translations remain accessible starting points, with vocabulary and interpretations that deserve comparison against current scholarship and original languages.

Priority gaps

Australian Aboriginal traditions; further African, Pacific and Indigenous American accounts; Southeast and Central Asia; Tibetan traditions; Zoroastrian and Bahá’í sources; additional Jewish, Christian, Hindu and Islamic schools; women’s intellectual histories; disability and neurodiversity; linguistics, psychiatry, dance and sport.

These require named communities, works and specialist or community-led sources. We will not fill the gaps with invented pan-cultural summaries.

Broad regional labels are navigation aids, not civilizational boundaries. Living traditions appear at the dates of the documented accounts used here. The nine recurring approaches are comparisons made by this project, not an indigenous classification or a ranking.
